title: Beloved, and told so (Avot 3:14)
hookLine: Akiva: every person is beloved, made in the image, and more beloved still for being told
tomorrow: if it's all foreseen, is anything really your choice?

cards: Somewhere in a drawer there's a card that says I'm proud of you, kept long after the birthday it came with. The words did something the love alone hadn't. Rabbi Akiva puts that in one line.
Beloved is a human being, created in the image. And an extra love: it was made known to them that they were created in the image. What's better than being loved?

teach.b: Akiva backs it with a verse from Genesis, the JPS words to Noah after the flood: "for in the image of God made He man." Those words are spoken to Noah's family, the ancestors of everyone.
Inside the tradition, two teachers argued over which verse is the Torah's great principle.
Akiva chose "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

teach.h: BEN AZZAI: ONE BOOK OF ADAM.
teach.b: His colleague Ben Azzai chose another: "This is the book of the generations of Adam," which goes on to say that God made the human in God's likeness. Hear each at its best.
Akiva: love starts with the person beside you, the one you can actually help today; a rule about all humanity can stay vague.

Ben Azzai: the word neighbor can shrink to people like me, and loving as yourself depends on how you treat yourself; one book of Adam puts every person in a single family, in God's likeness, with no exceptions.
The Sifra keeps both voices on the page.

And Akiva's own line in Avot seems to hold both: every human being is beloved, and the love has to be spoken to reach them. Avot goes on, in the same breath, to a second love: Israel, called children of God.

how: Jews learn Avot 3:14 alongside the Sifra's debate between Akiva and Ben Azzai; some families say a weekly blessing over their children on Friday night, telling them out loud that they are blessed.

o: dear, and dearer still for knowing it
chosen above others for a special task
forgiven in advance for every wrong

games.q: two great principles — tap the pairs.
p: the book of the generations of Adam

s: Akiva's verse about the image is spoken to Noah after the flood
'for in the image of God made He man' is Genesis 9:6.
the rabbis agreed on one great principle of the Torah
Akiva named love your neighbor; Ben Azzai named the book of the generations of Adam.
for Akiva, being loved is enough; being told adds nothing
an extra love is that it was made known.

games.q: a friend says love your neighbor is clearly the greatest rule. you're Ben Azzai. what's your best case for Genesis 5:1 instead?
o: neighbor can shrink to people like me; one book of Adam includes everyone.
loving yourself is selfish, so loving others as yourself is a weak rule.
Genesis comes first in the Torah, so its verse automatically wins.
games.why: Ben Azzai's verse puts every person in one family, in God's likeness. Akiva's starts with the person beside you. The Sifra keeps both.

practice: Think of someone who may not know how much they matter to you. Write them one plain sentence, not about what they did, but that you're glad they exist.
Send it, or keep it as a version for later; either way, let the sit be about them.

wordCard.voice: Beloved. Chaviv in Akiva's Hebrew: dear, and dearer still once it's been said.

orig.note: Hebrew: beloved, dear; Akiva's first word in Avot 3:14.

carryVoice: Beloved, and told so: love only reaches someone once it says itself out loud. Go gently.
